Remember

Choosing a technology is not a matter of “taste”: a wrong choice (for example a driven pile next to a sensitive neighbour, or unsupported drilling below the groundwater) can damage the surrounding buildings or result in a defective pile with discontinuities. That is why the soil and groundwater conditions must be known at the very start of design.

Deep-lying bearing stratum
A reliable bearing stratum lies only deeper – with soft clay, peat or fill above it.
Large loads
Towers, bridge piers, heavy industrial equipment: the upper layers could not carry the contact pressure.
Unacceptable settlement
With a shallow foundation the settlement would be too large or too uneven – for example for towers sensitive to tilting.
High groundwater table
A shallow foundation would need a watertight excavation and dewatering; overall a deep foundation is often more economical.
Scour, undermining
Around the river piers of bridges the water deepens the bed: the foundation must reach below the scour depth.
Risk of sliding
Under a strongly inclined load a shallow foundation could slide on its base; piles also take the horizontal force.

Prefabricated panel block
the 1970s–80s
shallow foundation or piles

A ten-storey prefabricated panel block is approx. 30 m tall. On good subsoil it stands on reinforced concrete strip or raft foundations approx. 2–3 m deep; on unfavourable subsoil it was founded on piles.
A point of reference: next to the other structures, the foundation of the panel block is almost invisible.
Wind turbine
onshore wind farm
reinforced concrete footing (on piles on weak soil)

The tower of a modern onshore wind turbine is approx. 100–150 m tall, and the blade tip reaches close to 200 m. Its foundation is typically a reinforced concrete footing approx. 15–25 m in diameter and 2–3 m thick, on piles on weak soil.
The tilt of the tower governs: the allowable differential settlement is approx. 3 mm/m.
reinforced concrete foundation taken down 15 m

For more than 30 years it was the tallest free-standing structure in the world. The load of the 553 m tall tower is transferred to the rock (shale) by a reinforced concrete foundation taken down 15 m.
If the bearing stratum is within reach, a massive foundation taken to depth is enough.
380 bored piles, approx. 80 m
The tower stands on 380 bored piles 1.5 m in diameter: they reach down approx. 80 m, socketed up to 30 m into the rock. The area is exposed to earthquakes and typhoons.
Large-diameter bored piles carry the load down to the deeper bearing stratum.
104 barrettes, 60–115 m

The bearing stratum lies very deep, so 104 reinforced concrete barrettes, 60–115 m long, were built for each tower, with a raft approx. 4.5 m thick on top. Measured from ground level, the foundation reaches approx. 120 m deep.
Unfavourable subsoil: most of the load is carried by shaft resistance.
Dubai, United Arab Emirates
192 bored piles, approx. 43 m + raft
The world’s tallest building stands on a reinforced concrete raft 3.7 m thick, supported by 192 bored piles 1.5 m in diameter and approx. 43 m long – a piled raft.
Almost twice as tall as the Petronas, yet it stands on much shorter piles: the depth of the foundation is set by the soil.
